children.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do
children.blurb: In the fall of 2023, nearly 1,000 students at a high school in Turkey took part in a simple test. During math review sessions, some students practiced with a plain AI chat tool, much like the free chatbots anyone can open on a phone.

children.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere
children.blurb: When this Volume began, the raw material was a stack of 1,200 ideas for using AI in schools, gathered from teachers, district leaders, researchers, and product lists. Reading them one by one felt like walking through a crowded market where every stall sold something slightly different.

children.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule
children.blurb: In June 2026, a school board member in Portland, Oregon, raised concerns about the data an AI reading assessment company would collect from students. The list of data fields in the company's contract included items such as place of birth and migrant status (Willamette Week, 2026).

children.name: Pilot, Measure, Scale
children.blurb: In a recent trial in Germany, 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools during six regular physics and English lessons. Some students got a tool designed to build motivation, some got a tool designed to teach learning strategies, and a comparison group used a plain chatbot.

sections.body: Getting Oriented is the opening part of the book's AI in Education section, and it is where the foundation for everything else is laid. In this part, the book explains what AI can and cannot do, the ten patterns that account for nearly every idea in the Volume, the laws and rules that protect students, and a simple method for piloting and measuring any new tool. It is not a set of activities or a tool review. It is the orientation that tells readers how to think about AI in school life before they try to use it. The book says readers who start nowhere else should start here.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that starting with these four chapters works because the rules set out in them apply to every idea in the chapters that follow. It treats the ten patterns as a way to account for nearly every idea in the Volume, so they are meant to be used again and again. It also holds to the laws and rules that protect students, including privacy, safety, and the Human Review Rule. The book does not present this part as a place to skip or to treat as separate from later practice. Its rule is that the foundation comes first and that later ideas must stay under the same rules.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a sequence from understanding to protection to testing. What AI Can and Cannot Do and Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere give the basic picture of AI's limits and the recurring ideas that appear across the Volume. Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule is where a leader or parent would go for the laws and rules that protect students and for the Human Review Rule. Pilot, Measure, Scale is where a leader or teacher would go for the simple method of trying and measuring any new tool. A teacher would likely start with What AI Can and Cannot Do and Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere, while a parent would likely start with Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule.
